title: 13 Lawmakers Seek Federal Probe Into Seattle Diwali Event Disruption
excerpt: All six Indian American House members signed a letter asking the Justice Department to examine whether two men who entered the Seattle Center Armory festival with racial slurs and anti-Hindu signs violated federal civil rights laws, with a briefing requested by December 4.
body:
• Thirteen members of the US House of Representatives — including all six Indian American members — have asked the Justice Department to investigate whether the November 7 disruption of a Diwali festival in Seattle violated federal civil rights laws.
  • The letter, led by Pramila Jayapal, Raja Krishnamoorthi and Grace Meng, names Jake Lang and Thomas Allen, who the lawmakers say entered the Seattle Center Armory celebration carrying signs with racial slurs and anti-Hindu messages.
  • The lawmakers cite three federal statutes — 18 U.S.C. sections 245, 241 and 247 — covering intimidation and interference, conspiracies against federal rights, and forcible obstruction of religious exercise. A request for an investigation is not a finding: the Justice Department has not publicly responded.
  • The date to watch is Friday, December 4, when the lawmakers have asked the Justice Department for a briefing on the incident and on efforts to prevent further hate against Indian American and South Asian American communities.

Thirteen US lawmakers have asked the Department of Justice to investigate whether the disruption of a Diwali celebration in Seattle was a federal civil rights violation, in a letter that puts every Indian American member of the House on the same page.

The letter, led by Representatives Pramila Jayapal, Raja Krishnamoorthi and Grace Meng, chair of the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus, follows the November 7 disruption at the Seattle Center Armory by two men carrying signs containing racial slurs and anti-Hindu messages, according to a statement released by Krishnamoorthi's office on Tuesday and reported by IANS. The event, "Diwali: Lights of India," was a free public festival of Indian classical dance, music, art and cultural activities, held as part of Seattle Center's Festál series at the Armory Food and Event Hall.

What the lawmakers are asking the Justice Department to test

The statement identified the two men as Jake Lang and Thomas Allen and said they entered the celebration carrying signs containing racist and hateful language; other reporting on the letter said one sign demanded the deportation of Indian Americans. The lawmakers urged the department to examine whether the men's actions violated federal protections against intimidation, interference with protected activities and obstruction of religious worship.

The request cites three statutes. Section 245 of Title 18 addresses intimidation or interference, by force or threat of force, based on race, religion, colour or national origin in connection with federally protected activities. Section 241 covers conspiracies to threaten or interfere with rights protected by the Constitution or federal law. Section 247 concerns the use of force or threats to obstruct a person's exercise of religious beliefs. The letter asks investigators to determine whether the conduct meets those tests — it does not establish that a federal offence occurred.

"It is vital that those of us entrusted with public offices confront hate wherever it appears. No family should have to wonder whether it is safe to light a lamp, perform a dance, or bring their children to a festival in their own city."

— The lawmakers' letter, via Krishnamoorthi's office

The wider pattern the letter cites

"The events in Seattle follow a troubling series of threats against South Asian communities across the country," the lawmakers wrote. Their letter cited a September 2026 study by the Centre for the Study of Organised Hate that identified more than 542,000 anti-South Asian hateful posts on X between January 2025 and June 2026, and said one in four Indian Americans report being called a slur since 2025.

The lawmakers also linked the incident to what they described as rhetoric from the Trump administration that had encouraged hostility toward South Asian communities, citing a Department of Homeland Security graphic mocking a Sikh driver. That contention is the lawmakers' allegation; a public response from the Justice Department or Homeland Security to the letter could not be located, IANS reported. The letter further asked the department to give greater priority to hate-crime investigations and to reinvest in its Community Relations Service, which helps communities resolve conflicts.

Besides Jayapal and Krishnamoorthi, the Indian American signatories were Ami Bera, Ro Khanna, Suhas Subramanyam and Shri Thanedar. The other signatories were Yassamin Ansari, Judy Chu, Suzan DelBene, Emily Randall, Lateefah Simon and Adam Smith, alongside Meng. The issue is live on the other coast as well: newly elected Congressman Amish Shah has put anti-Indian hate at the top of his agenda, as we reported in our coverage of his platform.

What happens next

The lawmakers have requested a briefing by December 4 on the Seattle incident and on federal efforts to prevent further acts of hate against Indian American and South Asian American communities. Whether the disruption is treated as a federal hate crime now rests with the Justice Department; as of Tuesday, it had made no public response.
